title: Seven are called
hookLine: on Shabbat morning seven people are called up to the Torah
last: A MOUTH AS FULL AS THE SEA.

cards: A name is called out across the sanctuary. Someone stands up, a little surprised, and makes their way to the front. A teenager who just turned thirteen.

A grandfather whose granddaughter was born this week. A woman about to be married, or a man who got out of the hospital on Tuesday. They step up to the open scroll, say a blessing, and stand there while a section is read.
Then the next name is called. On Shabbat morning, this happens seven times.

teach.b: Being called up is an aliyah, a going up. Same word as moving to the Land of Israel. You rise to the Torah.
The Mishnah, in tractate Megillah, sets the numbers, and they climb with the day.
On Monday and Thursday mornings, and Shabbat afternoon: three people. On the new moon and the middle days of festivals: four. On festivals: five.
On Yom Kippur: six. On Shabbat morning: seven. The more holy or restful the day, the more people get a turn.
Then, after the seven, one more is called for a closing section, and that person reads the haftarah, the prophets' portion we met a few weeks ago. Who goes first?

Traditionally a kohen, a descendant of the priests, then a Levite, then everyone else. The Mishnah gives the reason: for the sake of peace, so nobody fights over who goes first. Many congregations today keep that order.
Some don't. And in many congregations women are called as well as men; in Orthodox congregations, men are called. Later authorities describe a change.
Once, each person called up read their own section aloud. But not everyone could read the scroll, with no vowels and no punctuation.

teach.h: ONE READER, SO NO ONE IS SHAMED.
teach.b: To spare people embarrassment, the custom became that a trained reader reads for everyone, and the person called up says the blessings and follows along.
Seven people, one reader, a whole community in the passage. The portion is too big for one person to hold, so it's shared.

how: On Shabbat morning the Torah portion is divided into at least seven aliyot, plus the maftir; each person called up recites a blessing before and after while a trained reader chants the section. Many congregations call a kohen first and a Levite second, and people are often honored at life events.

o: only call those who can read.
have a trained reader read for everyone called.

practice: Picture a gathering you belong to, a service, a family dinner, a team, a choir, and count how many people actually have a role in it: who speaks, who serves, who carries, who cleans up.
Then picture someone at the edges who could be called up next time, and hold their face for a while.

wordCard.voice: Aliyah. A going up: being called to read from the Torah, as on Shabbat morning, when seven people take their turn.

orig.note: Hebrew: going up. being called to the Torah, and also moving to Israel.
